title: arXiv AI daily — 28 October 2026: five notable papers on agent reasoning and evaluation
global_caveat: arXiv has no official trending chart. This inferred shortlist is drawn from a 200-record recency sample; all five were less than two days old with zero Semantic Scholar citations at snapshot, and Hugging Face upvotes are a narrow platform-specific attention signal, not a readership measure or comprehensive ranking of the full batch.

sections.title: ThinkWorld: World Imagination Reinforces Chain-of-Dynamics Reasoning
sections.abstract: ThinkWorld represents actions as discrete Chains-of-Dynamics and uses predicted-versus-observed future states to train vision-language-action reasoning from robot demonstrations and videos without action labels.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors propose a shared motion-token reasoning space and consequence-grounded reinforcement learning, using future-state prediction to extend action supervision to unlabeled human videos; they report transfer to robots and generalization to unseen tasks and environments.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors report a single training seed, so episode-level confidence intervals do not measure variation across independently trained checkpoints; latency also depends on the stated hardware and input setup.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Hugging Face Papers displayed 48 upvotes at the snapshot, the highest among these five checked pages. The paper is cross-listed across robotics, AI, and vision and reports simulation and real-robot evaluations.

sections.title: Can LLMs Uncover Hidden Physical Laws through Free Exploration?
sections.abstract: LongChang tests whether LLM agents can investigate simulated worlds with altered physics and discover the hidden laws without being given research questions; only one of twelve evaluated models achieves a non-zero discovery rate.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors introduce LongChang, an automated altered-physics world and exploration-evaluation loop; their full results separate supported observations from correct law discovery, finding 97.6% evidence support but only 19.0% law correctness for the one model with discoveries.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors explicitly limit the study to simulated worlds with known altered laws and say extending it to unresolved real-world science requires further research; most evaluated models did not discover a law.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Hugging Face Papers displayed 7 upvotes at the snapshot. The paper is cross-listed in language, AI, and multiagent categories, and its project page provides a checkable research artifact.

sections.title: Timestral
sections.abstract: The authors introduce four probabilistic time-series foundation models from 5M to 209M parameters and report top results on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors combine Decoupled Horizon Forecasting, role-aware treatment of known-future covariates, and synthetic pretraining followed by mixed real-and-synthetic post-training; they report Timestral-209M ranking first among evaluated competitors on all three named suites.
sections.unique_caveat: The ranking is based on the paper’s evaluation of three public suites and its selected comparator set; it is not evidence of performance across all forecasting workloads or independent deployments.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Hugging Face Papers displayed 6 upvotes at the snapshot. The paper reports results on three forecasting benchmarks, provides model weights and inference code, and states that forecasts up to 1,024 steps are produced in one forward pass.

sections.title: Rare, Relevant, and Still Wrong: How Memory Fails LLM Group Decisions
sections.abstract: On a controlled 480-task benchmark, rarity- and relevance-based memory filters fail under different distributions of supporting and decoy facts, while attribution tags can induce social-proof errors in the final decision model.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors introduce CrossProfile and report that relevance filters can admit on-topic decoys, rarity-first selection is not better than random on average, and removing or randomizing agent-attribution tags can improve accuracy in the classic hidden-profile configuration.
sections.unique_caveat: The findings are bounded by the controlled hidden-profile benchmark, its four tested model families, and its fixed task construction; they do not establish how the same effects scale to arbitrary group discussions.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Hugging Face Papers displayed 5 upvotes at the snapshot. The paper is cross-listed across three core AI categories and introduces a 60-template benchmark separating fact ownership from fact content.

sections.title: TeamGym: A Gym for Team Decision-Making by AI Agents with Distributed Information
sections.abstract: TeamGym evaluates and trains language-model teams on decisions built from legal, finance, medical, and software corpora, measuring how distributing pivotal evidence affects communication and retrieval.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors define pivotal information and a configurable team benchmark; they report average success-rate drops of 22.9 percentage points when pivotal information is distributed across participants and a further 19.9 points when participants must retrieve it from source material, while two policy-training experiments improve coordination and final decisions.
sections.unique_caveat: Results are benchmark-based across the tested models and source corpora; transfer to live teams and other task distributions is not established.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Hugging Face Papers displayed 1 upvote at the snapshot. Its 8-model, 12-corpus study and controlled separation of communication from retrieval provide research-relevance evidence despite a small observed platform vote count.
